newsitem.title: FRANCE: Syria and France criticise Israeli housing move.
newsitem.headline: Syria and France criticise Israeli housing move.

text.p: France and Syria on Thursday criticised Israel's decision to build a new Jewish housing project in Arab East Jerusalem, saying it ran counter to Middle East peace.

Syrian Vice-President Abdel Halim Khaddam told reporters after a 90-minute meeting with French President Jacques Chirac: "In the light of Israel's recent initiatives, we can say that this country does not want peace.
"Syria wants peace, France wants peace, but Israel does not."

Chirac's spokeswoman Catherine Colonna said the French leader had voiced his concern after an Israeli cabinet committee approved plans to build 6,500 homes on Jabal Abu Ghneim, known by Israelis as Har Homa, in East Jerusalem on land captured in the 1967 Middle East war.
She said Chirac told Khaddam it was vital to relaunch Arab-Israeli peace negotiations and France was ready to make a contribution.

The president also expressed worries about an increase in violence in south Lebanon and called for restraint on all sides, including by Iranian-backed Hizbollah guerrillas who operate from areas controlled by Syrian troops.
Peace talks between Israel and Syria have been frozen since hardline Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was elected last May.

French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette, who is due to visit Syria, Lebanon and Israel from next Tuesday in hopes of promoting fresh negotiations, said the Israeli decision was a "very serious problem".
In a France-Inter radio interview, he said: "I believe this decision could create tension and difficulties because it is considered by the Palestinians as a violation of the (peace) arrangements."

Paris has been involved, in new-found harmony with the United States, in efforts to revive peace talks between the Jewish state, Damascus and Beirut. It has offered to join in policing the Israel-Lebanon border if a comprehensive agreement is reached.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt said: "This decision clearly breaches the status quo in Jerusalem, which must not change until the conclusion of negotiations on the final status (of the West Bank and Gaza Strip).
"This decision is thus contrary to the letter and spirit of the peace process," he told a briefing.

The Israeli move was all the more regrettable since the recent accord on a partial Israeli withdrawal from the West Bank city of Hebron had "helped restore confidence between the parties to the peace process and raised hopes of new progress".
